In practice, gemeenten cannot always provide an appointment within five days — but you should request one immediately and be able to demonstrate you tried to comply.

Failure to register on time does not usually result in a fine, but it does mean you cannot legally work, cannot get a BSN, cannot open a Dutch bank account, and cannot register for health insurance. The cascading consequences are severe enough that delay is rarely a good idea.

Booking the appointment

Each gemeente runs its own appointment system. For most cities, you book online at the gemeente's website. Amsterdam uses Amsterdam.nl with its dedicated Expat Center (located at the Stadsloket Centrum, Amstel 1). Rotterdam, The Hague, Utrecht, and Eindhoven all have similar online booking systems. Some smaller municipalities still operate on walk-in or telephone booking.

If you are arriving from outside the EU and need to register at the Expat Center in Amsterdam, you can sometimes book the appointment from abroad before you arrive — this is the fastest path. For other cities, you usually need a Dutch phone number or to book from inside the country.

What to bring

For all registrations: valid passport or, for EU citizens, national identity card; for non-EU nationals, your residence permit (verblijfsvergunning) or the IND letter confirming your application is in progress; proof of address — your rental contract, the keys, and ideally a recent utility bill in your name (you will not have one yet if you just arrived, but the rental contract is enough); a Dutch birth certificate with apostille if you were born outside the Netherlands and are registering for the first time — this is sometimes requested for non-EU nationals or in specific marital/family situations.

If you have children, bring their original birth certificates (with apostille and certified translation into Dutch, English, French, or German). If you are married, bring your marriage certificate (also with apostille and translation). The apostille requirement is universal for documents from countries party to the Hague Apostille Convention; for documents from countries not in the convention, full legalisation is needed instead — this is a longer process to start before you leave your home country.

What happens at the appointment

The appointment itself takes 30–45 minutes. A civil servant verifies your documents, takes your details, photographs your passport, and confirms your address. If everything is in order, you are issued your BSN on the spot — often as a paper certificate, sometimes by mailing it to your address within 5–10 business days, depending on the gemeente.

For non-EU nationals, the gemeente may also collect biometric information (fingerprints, signature) that gets associated with your residence permit. If you have not yet collected your physical residence permit from the IND, this is sometimes done at the same appointment.

The temporary address problem

The biggest practical obstacle to registration is the address requirement. Most gemeenten require a permanent or long-term address — a hotel, an Airbnb, or a friend's spare room is often not accepted. If you are staying with a friend or family member while you find permanent housing, you can sometimes register at their address with their written consent. The form for this is called a verklaring van inwoning and is available on the gemeente website. The host commits that you are genuinely living there, which has tax and benefit implications for them — many landlords (including private friends) are reluctant to sign.

Some short-stay providers (corporate housing, certain Airbnb hosts) explicitly allow registration; this is worth verifying before signing. The Amsterdam Expat Center is somewhat more flexible than other gemeenten about temporary addresses for highly skilled migrants.

After you register

Once registered, your BSN is generated. With the BSN, complete the rest of the setup sequence in this order: take out Dutch health insurance (within four months of arrival), open a Dutch bank account at ABN AMRO or ING (online with BSN takes 1–2 days), apply for DigiD at digid.nl (activation letter takes 5 days), and notify your employer of your BSN so payroll is correctly registered.

Changing address

If you move within the Netherlands later, you must update your registration with your new gemeente within five days of moving — same rule. This is done online via the new gemeente's website using your DigiD. Moving abroad permanently requires emigratie deregistration; this is also done with the gemeente before leaving and is important because it stops Dutch tax residency.

If you have no permanent address yet

The registration requires an address, which creates an obvious problem for anyone still house-hunting — and Dutch rental markets rarely accommodate a five-day timeline. Our Amsterdam rental guide covers why.

Two routes exist. Some gemeenten will register you at a friend's or landlord's address with that person's written consent, provided you genuinely live there. Failing that, a briefadres (correspondence address) can be granted in defined circumstances — it gives you a registration for official mail without asserting you live at that address. Availability varies by municipality and it is not a general-purpose workaround, so ask your specific gemeente rather than assuming.

What you should not do is register at an address you do not actually live at. Address fraud is treated seriously, the person whose address you use may face consequences too, and municipalities do conduct checks.

Moving house, and the same five days again

The five-day rule is not only an arrival rule. Every time you move within the Netherlands you must notify your gemeente within five days — and if you move to a different municipality, you register with the new one, which handles the transfer.

This one is easy to overlook because nothing obviously breaks at first. What follows later is worse: mail from the Belastingdienst, your insurer, and the IND goes to an old address, and "I did not receive the letter" is not a defence against a missed deadline. Most gemeenten now allow an address change online with DigiD, which takes minutes.

Deregistering when you leave

The step almost nobody plans for. If you leave the Netherlands for more than eight months in any twelve, you must deregister (uitschrijven), generally within five days of departure.

Deregistering matters in both directions. Staying registered while living abroad can keep you inside the Dutch tax and health-insurance system, continuing to accrue premium obligations for cover you cannot use. Deregistering carelessly can strand you: it may terminate health insurance, benefits and allowances from that date, and it affects any residence permit or naturalisation clock you have been building. Our citizenship guide explains why continuous registration matters for naturalisation.

Before you go: settle your final tax return, keep a Dutch bank account open until refunds land, and give the Belastingdienst a forwarding address.

Common document problems

Almost every delayed registration traces to paperwork, and almost always to the same three issues. Apostilles take longer than expected — start birth and marriage certificate legalisation before you leave your home country, not after you arrive. Translations must be by a sworn translator; an ordinary translation is routinely refused. And name discrepancies between passport and certificates — transliteration differences, patronymics, married names — need resolving with the issuing authority, which is slow from abroad.

If a document genuinely cannot be obtained, gemeenten can sometimes accept a sworn statement instead, but this is discretionary and much smoother if you raise it before the appointment rather than at the desk.

faq.q: When do I have to register at the gemeente?
faq.a: Within five days of arriving if you will stay longer than four months. Gemeenten cannot always offer an appointment that quickly, so request one immediately and be able to show you tried to comply.

faq.q: What documents do I need to bring?
faq.a: A valid passport or EU ID (or your residence permit/IND letter if non-EU), and proof of address such as your rental contract. For a first registration or family members, apostilled birth or marriage certificates with a certified translation are sometimes required.

faq.q: Can I register at a temporary address?
faq.a: Often it is difficult — many gemeenten require a permanent address, so a hotel or Airbnb may not be accepted. You can sometimes register at a friend's address with a signed verklaring van inwoning, though hosts are frequently reluctant. Verify that any short-stay provider allows registration before signing.

faq.q: What's the difference between BRP and RNI registration?
faq.a: BRP is the residents' register, for stays over four months — it gives you a BSN and an official Dutch address. RNI is the non-residents' register for shorter stays: you still get a BSN, enough to be paid and taxed, but no registered address, which limits banking and other admin. If a short stay becomes a long one, you must switch — it doesn't happen automatically.

faq.q: Do I need to do anything when I move house within the Netherlands?
faq.a: Yes — notify your gemeente within five days, same as on arrival. If you move to a different municipality you register with the new one. Nothing obviously breaks if you skip it, which is why people do; the consequence arrives later when Belastingdienst or IND post goes to your old address, and not receiving a letter is not a defence against a missed deadline.

faq.q: What happens if I leave the Netherlands — do I need to deregister?
faq.a: If you're away more than eight months in any twelve, yes, generally within five days of leaving. Staying registered can keep you inside the Dutch tax and health insurance system, accruing premiums for cover you can't use. But deregistering also ends allowances and affects any residence-permit or naturalisation clock, so time it deliberately.

title: The inburgering exam in the Netherlands: who needs it and how to pass
excerpt: Integration is a legal obligation with a three-year deadline for most non-EU newcomers, and the language bar is rising to B1. Here's who must sit it, who's exempt, what the exams involve, what it costs, and what happens — including to your residence status — if you miss the deadline.
body:
Inburgering — civic integration — is the Netherlands’ formal requirement for non-EU residents to demonstrate a basic command of Dutch language and knowledge of Dutch society. Many expats encounter it as a surprise: they have lived and worked in the country for a year or two, and then a letter from Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs (DUO) arrives, giving them three years to pass a series of exams. Understanding who must comply, what the exams involve, and how the 2026 rules have changed is essential for anyone planning a long-term stay.

Who must integrate — and who is exempt

The obligation under the Wet inburgering 2021 applies to non-EU/EEA nationals who hold a residence permit for a non-temporary purpose — most commonly family reunification permits, partner-of-expat permits, and humanitarian protection permits. EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals are exempt, as are Turkish nationals in most cases under the Ankara Agreement. Highly skilled migrants (kennismigranten) and European Blue Card holders are exempt while they hold those specific permit categories, though the requirement can become relevant if they later apply for a permanent permit or Dutch citizenship.

Further exemptions apply to people over the pension age (67 years and 10 months), those with serious certified health conditions or disabilities, and anyone who already holds a qualifying Dutch language diploma — such as an NT2 Staatsexamen diploma or a Dutch secondary or higher-education degree. If you believe you qualify for a vrijstelling (exemption), apply to DUO as soon as possible. The three-year deadline does not pause automatically while an exemption application is pending.

The 2026 language requirement: B1

The Wet inburgering 2021, which applied from January 2022 onward, set B1 Dutch as the standard integration target — roughly the level needed to hold a functional conversation, read straightforward news articles, and manage a workplace discussion. Municipalities (gemeenten) can authorise an A2 track in exceptional cases where B1 is demonstrably unattainable, but A2 is no longer the default. For anyone whose obligation began after 2022, assume B1 unless DUO or your gemeente indicates otherwise.

In 2026, B1 also matters for naturalisation. Legislation expected later this year is likely to make B1 the firm minimum for Dutch citizenship applications. Those who passed at A2 before the change may be protected by transitional provisions, but the window for relying on an A2 diploma for citizenship purposes is closing. Anyone planning to naturalise in the next few years would be wise to aim for B1 from the outset.

What the exam consists of

Under the Wet inburgering 2021, integration involves five assessed components: separate exams in Dutch speaking, listening, reading, and writing (each at B1, or A2 if authorised), plus the Kennis van de Nederlandse Maatschappij (KNM) exam covering Dutch society, institutions, and civic expectations. The KNM exam was substantially updated in July 2025 — it now focuses on practical situational scenarios rather than theoretical fact recall, testing how you would handle a conversation at a government desk, a parent-teacher meeting, or a medical appointment. The speaking exam also changed in 2025: the multiple-choice section was removed and all questions are now spoken, which requires active preparation rather than pattern recognition. The sixth and final requirement is the Participatieverklaring — a brief ceremony at your gemeente where you sign a declaration affirming respect for Dutch civic values. No language examination is involved.

Costs, timeline, and practical steps

Each exam costs approximately €50, payable to DUO. With five exams (and possibly resits), total exam fees typically fall in the €250–€400 range. Preparation is the main financial variable: a certified B1 language course costs €1,500–€3,000 depending on provider and intensity. DUO offers a taalbudget — a loan of up to €10,000 for integration-related education — available at language schools holding the Blik op Werk keurmerk quality mark. The loan is repaid from income once your integration is complete.

The three-year deadline from the date of your obligation letter is enforced. Failure to complete integration by the deadline can result in a fine of up to €1,250 and may block conversion of a temporary residence permit to a permanent one. Extensions for exceptional circumstances must be requested proactively — contact DUO before the deadline rather than after. For a complete beginner, reaching B1 requires an estimated 500–600 hours of study — roughly one year of part-time evening classes. Starting within the first year of your obligation letter is strongly advisable. If your long-term goal is a permanent residence permit or Dutch citizenship, beginning language study as early as possible in your Dutch life makes the path considerably smoother.

Who pays, and the loan that has to be repaid

Under the current system, responsibility differs sharply depending on how you came to the Netherlands. Municipalities lead the process for asylum-status holders and generally arrange and fund provision. Most other obliged newcomers — family migrants in particular — arrange their own course and carry the cost.

A government loan is available through DUO to cover tuition and exam fees, and it is genuinely useful, but it is a loan. Repayment terms depend on your route and on meeting your deadline; failing to integrate in time can mean repaying in full alongside a fine. Treat it as debt with conditions attached, not a grant.

Choosing a school, and the quality problem

Course quality varies considerably, and the market has had problems with providers optimising for enrolment rather than results. Look for the Blik op Werk quality mark, which is the recognised standard and is generally required for DUO loan funding.

Before committing, ask three questions: what pass rates does the school achieve at the level you need, how large are the classes, and does the timetable actually fit around your work? A cheap course you cannot attend is more expensive than a good one you can.

What happens if you miss the deadline

The obligation carries a deadline, normally three years, and consequences for missing it are real: a fine, a requirement to repay the DUO loan, and — most seriously — consequences for your residence status. Passing the integration requirement is a precondition for a permanent residence permit and for Dutch citizenship, so a missed deadline does not merely cost money, it stalls your longer-term status.

Extensions can be granted where there is genuine cause — illness, pregnancy, demonstrable inability to study, or being let down by a failing provider — but they are applied for, not automatic, and evidenced. If you can see the deadline slipping, act months ahead rather than after it passes.

Exemptions and the diploma route

Some people are exempt without sitting anything. EU, EEA and Swiss nationals are not subject to the obligation. Certain Dutch or Belgian-Dutch-language qualifications provide exemption, and a documented medical condition preventing study can too.

There is also the shortcut worth checking before enrolling anywhere: passing a higher-level state language exam, or holding certain Dutch-taught qualifications, can satisfy the requirement outright. If your Dutch is already strong, sitting the higher exam directly can be faster and cheaper than a full course — and it leaves you better placed for the language level required for naturalisation.

faq.q: Who has to do the inburgering exam?
faq.a: Non-EU/EEA nationals on a non-temporary permit — most commonly family reunification, partner-of-expat, and humanitarian permits. EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals are exempt, as are highly skilled migrants and EU Blue Card holders while they hold those permits.

faq.q: What level and which exams are required?
faq.a: B1 Dutch has been the standard target since 2022. The components are separate exams in speaking, listening, reading, and writing, plus the Knowledge of Dutch Society (KNM) exam and the Participatieverklaring (a short declaration ceremony at your gemeente).

faq.q: What are the deadline and costs?
faq.a: You generally have three years from your DUO obligation letter; missing it risks a fine of up to €1,250 and can block a permanent permit. Each exam costs about €50, and a certified B1 course runs €1,500–€3,000 — DUO offers a loan of up to €10,000 for integration education.

faq.q: Who pays for the integration course?
faq.a: It depends on your route. Municipalities generally arrange and fund provision for asylum-status holders; most other obliged newcomers, family migrants especially, arrange and pay for their own. A DUO loan covers tuition and exam fees — but it is a loan, and missing your deadline can mean repaying in full plus a fine.

faq.q: What happens if I miss the integration deadline?
faq.a: A fine, repayment of the DUO loan, and consequences for your residence status — integration is a precondition for permanent residence and for Dutch citizenship, so a missed deadline stalls your longer-term position. Extensions exist for genuine cause such as illness or a failing provider, but must be applied for with evidence, ideally months ahead.

faq.q: Can I skip the course if my Dutch is already good?
faq.a: Often yes. Passing a higher-level state language exam, or holding certain Dutch-taught qualifications, can satisfy the requirement outright. If your Dutch is already strong this is usually faster and cheaper than a full course, and it leaves you better placed for the level required for naturalisation.

title: Working as a ZZP freelancer in the Netherlands: the expat guide
excerpt: Registering as a ZZP'er is simple; staying compliant is less so. The freelancer deduction has been cut to €1.200, the 1,225-hour criterion gates it, and from 2026 the Belastingdienst actively inspects for false self-employment. Here's the full picture before you leave employment.
body:
The Netherlands has one of the largest self-employed workforces in the EU — roughly 1.2 million ZZP'ers (zelfstandigen zonder personeel, self-employed without staff), a significant share of them international. The appeal is real: registration is genuinely simple, the market for skilled contractors is deep, and the tax system has historically been generous to early-stage freelancers.

Two things have changed that calculus. The headline freelancer deduction has been cut sharply through a multi-year phasedown, and from January 2026 the Belastingdienst began actively enforcing rules against false self-employment. Anyone considering this route needs the current picture, not the one that circulated a few years ago.

What ZZP status actually is

A ZZP'er trades as a sole trader (eenmanszaak): no minimum capital, no incorporation, minimal formality. You invoice clients, and you are responsible for your own tax, insurance and pension.

The critical structural point is that an eenmanszaak has no legal separation between you and the business. Business debts are your debts, and your personal assets are exposed. This is the main argument for eventually incorporating as a BV (the Dutch private limited company), which does create that separation but brings corporation tax, mandatory director's salary rules, statutory accounts and materially higher accountancy costs. The conventional wisdom is that a BV starts making sense somewhere around a sustained profit in the region of €100,000, but liability exposure in your particular line of work can justify it earlier.

The immigration question, first

Before anything else: you must hold the right to work in the Netherlands as a self-employed person. EU, EEA and Swiss nationals have this automatically.

For non-EU nationals this is the step that most often goes wrong. The standard kennismigrant (highly skilled migrant) permit is tied to a sponsoring employer and does not generally permit self-employment. Moving from employment to freelancing requires a separate IND application and approval before you begin trading. Registering a business you are not permitted to operate creates an immigration problem considerably worse than the tax problem it looks like.

Some residence permits — including certain partner and permanent residence permits — do carry unrestricted work rights. Check the specific endorsement on your own permit rather than reasoning from someone else's situation.

Registering with the KvK

Registration with the Kamer van Koophandel is free and done by appointment at a KvK office. Bring passport or ID, proof of your Dutch address, your BSN, and your residence permit if applicable.

You leave with a KvK number the same day. Within roughly two weeks the Belastingdienst issues your VAT identification number (btw-identificatienummer), which must appear on invoices to Dutch business clients. You will also be asked to choose an SBI activity code describing what you do — worth a moment's thought, since it can affect how your work is classified.

The urencriterium: the condition behind the deductions

This is the requirement most often missed, and it gates the most valuable reliefs. To claim the zelfstandigenaftrek and the startersaftrek, you must satisfy the urencriterium: at least 1,225 hours spent on your business in the calendar year.

Several details matter. The threshold is not pro-rated — start trading in October and you still need the full 1,225 hours in that year, which is effectively impossible, so first-year timing affects what you can claim. The hours are not only billable hours: administration, marketing, quoting, bookkeeping and professional development all count, which is more generous than people assume. And if you also hold a job, there is an additional requirement that the majority of your working time goes to the business — a constraint that catches part-time freelancers with a main employer.

You must be able to evidence the hours. A contemporaneous log — even a simple spreadsheet kept weekly — is what the Belastingdienst expects. Reconstructing a year of hours after an enquiry has begun is not a strong position.

The 2026 false self-employment enforcement

From 1 January 2026 the Belastingdienst began actively inspecting ZZP arrangements for schijnzelfstandigheid — engagements that are functionally employment dressed as contracting. The concern is companies avoiding social contributions, sick pay and dismissal protection.

The test is independence. Risk signals include working for a single client over an extended period, working under the same supervision as that client's employees, doing work indistinguishable from permanent staff, and rates below roughly €38 per hour, at which point a legal presumption of employment arises and the burden shifts to the client to rebut it.

Consequences fall primarily on the hiring company, which is why the practical effect on freelancers has been indirect but real: some clients have become reluctant to engage ZZP'ers at all, or now insist on contract terms and working practices that demonstrate independence. Protective habits are worth adopting — maintain several clients, keep your own equipment and working methods, avoid job titles and internal structures that imply staff status, and use a written contract that describes a deliverable rather than a role.

Tax and the deductions that remain

You pay income tax on net profit through the annual return, at ordinary Box 1 rates — approximately 36.97% up to €75,518 and 49.5% above.

Against that sit three reliefs. The zelfstandigenaftrek is €1,200 in 2026, down from €2,470 in 2025 as part of a deliberate phasedown — a change that has substantially reduced the tax advantage of freelancing and is worth factoring into any comparison with salaried work. The startersaftrek adds €2,123 in up to three of your first five years. The MKB-winstvrijstelling then exempts a further 12.7% of remaining profit. On a €60,000 profit these together reduce taxable income by roughly €11,000.

The first two require the urencriterium. The MKB-winstvrijstelling does not, which makes it the one relief a part-time freelancer can still count on.

Set money aside as you invoice. Unlike employment there is no withholding, and the combined income tax and health insurance contribution bill arriving after year end is the classic first-year shock. A reserve of roughly 35–45% of profit is a common rule of thumb.

VAT: returns, the KOR, and reverse charge

Most ZZP'ers file VAT returns quarterly through Mijn Belastingdienst, charging the standard rate on Dutch sales and reclaiming input VAT on business purchases.

The kleineondernemersregeling (KOR) exempts traders with turnover below €20,000 from charging VAT and from quarterly filing — at the cost of not reclaiming input VAT. It suits low-overhead service businesses and works against you if you are buying equipment. Note it binds you for a period once elected, so it is not a decision to flip annually.

If your clients are businesses in other EU countries, VAT typically reverse-charges to the client, meaning you invoice without Dutch VAT but must state their VAT number and file the associated EU sales listing. Clients outside the EU are generally outside the scope of Dutch VAT. Cross-border VAT is where freelance bookkeeping most often goes wrong — worth getting right at the outset rather than unpicking later.

Invoicing, admin and getting paid

Dutch invoices must carry specific particulars: your name and address, KvK and VAT numbers, the client's details, a sequential invoice number, the date, a description, and the VAT treatment. You are required to retain your records for seven years.

The standard payment term is 30 days unless agreed otherwise, and Dutch law entitles you to statutory interest and a fixed collection charge on late payment. Freelancers routinely fail to invoke this. A polite reminder citing the entitlement is often enough, and for persistent non-payment the small claims route through the kantonrechter is accessible without a lawyer for modest sums.

The safety net you no longer have

Basic health insurance remains mandatory. Beyond that you are uninsured by default, and this is the most serious and most ignored aspect of Dutch self-employment.

There is no state sickness or disability cover for ZZP'ers — the WIA system applies to employees only. If illness stops you working, income stops. Private disability insurance (AOV) typically runs €150–€350 a month depending on age, occupation and terms; a broodfonds is a cheaper mutual alternative covering shorter absences. Our AOV guide compares the options, and a long-postponed mandatory scheme remains in political discussion.

Pension is the same story: no employer contribution, no automatic scheme. Tax-advantaged routes exist for self-employed pension saving, and the practical risk is not that they are unavailable but that a decade passes without anyone prompting you to use them.

Getting started, in order

Confirm your permit allows self-employment; book a KvK appointment; register; open a separate business bank account; set up bookkeeping before your first invoice rather than after your first quarter; and start an hours log on day one. Online bookkeeping services run roughly €50–€150 a month and are generally worth it if the Dutch-language Belastingdienst portal is unfamiliar territory.

Do the arithmetic honestly before leaving employment. With the zelfstandigenaftrek reduced to €1,200, and with disability cover and pension now your own cost, the gross rate required to match a salaried package is higher than the headline comparison suggests.

faq.q: How do I register as a ZZP freelancer?
faq.a: Book a free KvK appointment and bring passport or ID, proof of Dutch address, your BSN and residence permit if applicable. You get a KvK number the same day, and the Belastingdienst issues your VAT number within about two weeks. Confirm your permit allows self-employment before you do any of this.

faq.q: Can non-EU nationals work as a freelancer?
faq.a: Only with a permit that specifically allows self-employment. The standard kennismigrant permit is tied to a sponsoring employer and generally does not, so moving to freelancing requires a separate IND application approved before you start trading. Registering a business you aren't permitted to run creates an immigration problem, not just a tax one.

faq.q: What is the urencriterium and why does it matter?
faq.a: You must spend at least 1,225 hours on your business in the calendar year to claim the zelfstandigenaftrek and startersaftrek. It isn't pro-rated, so starting in October effectively rules it out for that year. Admin, marketing and bookkeeping count, not just billable work — but you need a contemporaneous log to evidence it.

faq.q: What is the 2026 schijnzelfstandigheid crackdown?
faq.a: From January 2026 the Belastingdienst actively inspects whether ZZP arrangements are genuine self-employment or disguised employment. Risk signals include a single long-term client, working under the same supervision as staff, and rates below roughly €38/hour, where a legal presumption of employment applies. Consequences fall mainly on the client, which is why some have become reluctant to engage freelancers.

faq.q: What happens if I get sick as a ZZP'er?
faq.a: Nothing, unless you have arranged cover yourself. There is no state sickness or disability benefit for the self-employed — WIA covers employees only. Private AOV runs roughly €150–€350 a month; a broodfonds is a cheaper mutual alternative for shorter absences. This is the most commonly ignored risk in Dutch freelancing.

faq.q: Is it still worth going freelance in 2026?
faq.a: The maths is tighter than it was. The zelfstandigenaftrek has fallen to €1,200 from €2,470 in 2025 as part of a phasedown, and disability cover and pension are your own cost. The gross rate needed to match a salaried package is meaningfully higher than a simple day-rate comparison suggests — do that arithmetic before resigning.

title: Parental leave in the Netherlands: the expat guide
excerpt: Dutch parental leave combines several separate schemes, most paid at a percentage rather than in full. Here's how maternity, partner and parental leave stack up, what your CAO might top up, and the 30% ruling threshold that a period of leave can quietly push you below.
body:
Parental leave in the Netherlands is generous by international standards but more complex than most expats expect. There are three separate leave types — maternity leave, partner leave, and parental leave — each with its own duration, payment rules, and application process. Knowing what applies to whom, and in what order, is essential before a due date approaches.

Maternity leave (zwangerschaps- en bevallingsverlof)

The birth mother is entitled to a minimum of 16 weeks of paid maternity leave: typically four to six weeks before the due date and ten to twelve weeks after the birth, with at least ten weeks post-birth guaranteed regardless of when the leave started. Payment is at 100 per cent of your average daily wage, capped at the maximum daily wage set by the Dutch government — in 2026, approximately €290.67 per day. For most employees this means full pay; for higher earners whose gross daily wage exceeds the cap, there is a slight shortfall.

Payment flows through the UWV (Uitvoeringsinstituut Werknemersverzekeringen, the Dutch employee insurance agency). Your employer claims the UWV benefit on your behalf and continues paying your salary normally; you do not deal with UWV directly. The only requirement on your side is notifying your employer of your intended leave start date at least three weeks in advance.

Maternity leave applies to any employee covered by Dutch social security — meaning anyone working for a Dutch employer or a foreign employer based in the Netherlands. Nationality does not matter. If you see Dutch social insurance premiums (WW, WIA, ZW) being deducted from your payslip, you are entitled to maternity leave on exactly the same terms as a Dutch employee.

Partner leave (partnerverlof)

The non-gestational partner is entitled to two forms of leave following the birth. The first is one week of geboorteverlof (birth leave) — five working days — which must be taken within four weeks of the birth and is paid at 100 per cent of salary by the employer. This is a statutory entitlement and cannot be refused on operational grounds.

The second is aanvullend geboorteverlof (additional birth leave) of up to five weeks, which must be taken within six months of the birth. UWV pays 70 per cent of the partner's daily wage during this period, up to the same daily cap. The partner applies directly to UWV using their DigiD at least four weeks before the leave starts. Some employers voluntarily top up the 70 per cent to full salary — worth checking your employment contract before the birth.

Parental leave (ouderschapsverlof)

Both parents are entitled to 26 weeks of parental leave per parent, available at any point until the child turns eight. This is separate from and in addition to the maternity and partner leave described above. The 26 weeks can be taken in one block, in separate periods, or by reducing working hours across a longer span.

Since August 2022, the first nine weeks of parental leave — if taken within the first year after the child's birth — are paid by UWV at 70 per cent of your daily wage, up to a maximum of €212.97 per day in 2026. The remaining 17 weeks are unpaid unless your employer voluntarily tops them up. To access the paid portion you must take those nine weeks before the child's first birthday; parental leave taken after that point is unpaid.

To take parental leave, notify your employer in writing at least two months before the start date, specifying the hours per week and duration. An employer cannot refuse parental leave on operational grounds, though they can postpone it by up to four weeks in exceptional circumstances.

How the 30% ruling interacts with leave

The 30% ruling does not affect your entitlement to any form of parental or maternity leave. However, UWV calculates benefits based on your taxable wage — the 70 per cent portion of your gross salary — not your full gross. For 30% ruling holders on higher salaries, this means the effective replacement rate of the UWV benefit may be lower than it appears at first glance. Understand this calculation before planning an extended leave period if your household budget depends on the full replacement income.

Practical steps and applications

For maternity leave, inform your employer in writing at least three weeks before the intended start date; your employer files with UWV on your behalf. For additional partner leave (the five-week block), apply directly at uwv.nl using your DigiD at least four weeks before the leave starts — you will need your employer's details and your BSN. For parental leave, submit written notice to your employer at least two months in advance; if taking the paid nine-week portion in the first year, your employer files the UWV application. Keep copies of all correspondence. Dutch employment law protects employees strongly in these situations, but written records matter if any dispute arises.

If you are self-employed (ZZP)

Self-employed ZZP'ers have access to a separate maternity provision through the UWV's ZEZ scheme (Zwangerschapsuitkering voor Zelfstandigen). A self-employed mother can claim 16 weeks of maternity benefit at 100 per cent of declared profit, up to the daily cap, and must apply to UWV at least two weeks before the leave starts. The paid additional partner leave and the paid nine weeks of parental leave introduced in 2022 for employees do not apply to ZZP'ers — they receive only the unpaid parental leave entitlement unless they have taken out supplementary private insurance.

How the leaves stack up over a first year

The Dutch entitlements are separate schemes with separate rules, and their value comes from combining them rather than reading each in isolation.

In broad shape: the birthing parent takes pregnancy and maternity leave around the birth; the partner takes a short fully paid partner leave immediately, followed by additional partner leave paid at a percentage through the UWV; and both parents then hold an individual parental leave entitlement, partly paid if taken within the child's first year and unpaid thereafter, usable until the child turns eight.

The planning consequence is that the partly-paid window is time-limited while the entitlement itself is not. Couples who spread parental leave across the first year capture the paid portion; couples who defer it to year three still have the leave but lose the payment. Deciding this in the first months, rather than drifting, is worth real money.

Paid at a percentage, not in full

Most of these schemes pay a proportion of salary via the UWV rather than full pay, and there is a statutory maximum daily wage that caps benefit regardless of what you earn. For higher earners this is a significant reduction.

Two things soften it. Many collective labour agreements top payments up, sometimes to full salary — check your CAO before assuming the statutory minimum applies, because sector agreements vary widely. And because the payments run through the UWV, your employer normally applies on your behalf, which means the practical failure mode is nobody applying at all rather than an application being refused.

Ask HR explicitly what they are submitting and when. Deadlines apply, and an unclaimed entitlement is not usually recoverable later.

Watch the 30% ruling salary threshold

The interaction expats miss most. The 30% ruling requires your taxable salary to stay above a threshold, tested annually — and a period of leave paid at a percentage of salary can pull your annual figure under it.

Losing the ruling for a year is expensive and not always recoverable. If you are planning extended leave, raise it with payroll before it starts: how leave is structured, timed, or topped up can determine whether the threshold is met. This is a specific, avoidable trap, and payroll departments will generally engage with it if asked in advance.

Childcare: start before the leave ends

Daycare waiting lists in the major cities run to a year or more, so the practical sequencing is to register with several providers during pregnancy rather than as leave ends. Our childcare allowance guide covers the funding, which meets a substantial share of the cost for working parents — but the allowance is irrelevant if you have no place.

Registration is generally free or nominal, and holding several options costs little. The failure mode here is not financial; it is a parent unable to return to work because no place exists.

faq.q: How much maternity leave is there?
faq.a: The birth mother is entitled to at least 16 weeks, paid at 100% of average daily wage up to a cap (about €290.67 per day in 2026). The benefit flows through the UWV, but your employer claims it and keeps paying your salary, so you do not deal with UWV directly.

faq.q: What leave does the partner get?
faq.a: One week of birth leave at 100% of salary (within four weeks of the birth), plus up to five weeks of additional birth leave at 70% (within six months). The partner applies directly to the UWV using DigiD at least four weeks before the leave starts.

faq.q: What is the parental leave entitlement?
faq.a: Each parent gets 26 weeks of parental leave, usable until the child turns eight. The first nine weeks are paid at 70% (max €212.97 per day in 2026) if taken within the first year; the remaining weeks are unpaid unless your employer tops them up.

faq.q: Can taking parental leave cost me the 30% ruling?
faq.a: It can. The ruling requires your taxable salary to stay above a threshold, tested annually, and leave paid at a percentage of salary can pull your annual figure under it. Losing it for a year is expensive and not always recoverable. Raise planned leave with payroll before it starts — timing and structure can determine whether the threshold is met.

faq.q: Is parental leave paid in full?
faq.a: Usually not. Most schemes pay a proportion of salary through the UWV, capped by a statutory maximum daily wage, which bites for higher earners. Many collective labour agreements top this up, sometimes to full pay, so check your CAO rather than assuming the statutory minimum. Your employer normally applies on your behalf — confirm they actually have.

faq.q: When should I arrange childcare?
faq.a: During pregnancy, not as leave ends. Daycare waiting lists in the major cities routinely run a year or more. Registration is usually free or nominal, so put your name down with several providers. The allowance covers much of the cost for working parents, but it's irrelevant if there's no place available.

title: Sick leave in the Netherlands: your rights and your employer's obligations
excerpt: Dutch sick leave protection is among Europe's strongest — up to two years of pay and dismissal protection. Here's what you must do on day one, your right to medical privacy, the reintegration timeline, how to contest the company doctor, and what long-term illness means for your residence permit.
body:
Being ill is unavoidable, and understanding what to do when it happens — and what your employer is legally required to do — can make an already difficult period considerably less stressful. Dutch employment law offers some of the strongest sick leave protections in Europe, but the system comes with specific rules, timelines, and obligations that every expat employee should know before they need them.

Calling in sick: what you must do on day one

In the Netherlands, you are required to notify your employer of your illness as soon as possible on the first day of absence — typically before your normal start time. This notification is known as a ziekmelding. Most employers specify the preferred method: a telephone call to your direct manager is standard, and many employers explicitly do not accept a text message or email as a first contact. Your employer may ask you to state your expected duration of absence and a contact number, but that is all they are legally permitted to request. You are not required to name or describe your illness, and under Dutch privacy law — the Wet bescherming persoonsgegevens and the European GDPR — your employer is not allowed to record your diagnosis.

How much you are paid during sick leave

Dutch law guarantees a minimum of 70 per cent of your last-earned wage for up to two years of illness, though during the first year this 70 per cent must be at least equal to the statutory minimum wage (minimumloon). In practice, many collective labour agreements (CAO) are more generous: it is common for the first year of illness to be paid at 100 per cent and the second year at 70 per cent, though this depends on your sector and your individual employment contract. If your contract is silent on the matter and no CAO applies, the statutory minimum of 70 per cent applies from day one. There is no waiting period — unlike some countries, Dutch law does not allow employers to impose unpaid days at the start of a sick period.

Your right to privacy

One of the most significant protections in the Dutch system is the strict separation between your employer and your medical information. Your employer cannot ask what is wrong with you, cannot require you to provide a doctor's note as a condition of continued pay, and cannot record your diagnosis in any company system. When a company doctor (bedrijfsarts) becomes involved — which typically happens around the sixth week of illness — that doctor works independently and communicates with your employer only in terms of what you are functionally capable of doing, not why. This means your employer may learn that you are unable to sit for prolonged periods, but not that you have a back injury or are receiving treatment for depression.

What happens after six weeks: the reintegration process

If you are still unwell after six weeks, your employer is required to draw up a plan van aanpak — an action plan — together with you, outlining steps towards recovery and return to work. A company doctor must have assessed you by this point. At 42 weeks of continuous illness, your employer must formally notify the UWV, the Dutch Employee Insurance Agency. Throughout the two-year period, both you and your employer have active reintegration obligations: your employer must explore whether you can return to your own role (spoor 1) and, if not, whether alternative work can be found at another employer (spoor 2). Failure by your employer to document and pursue reintegration properly can result in the UWV imposing a wage sanction, forcing your employer to continue paying your salary for an additional 52 weeks beyond the normal two-year limit.

Job protection during illness

For the duration of your sick leave — up to two years — your employer is prohibited from dismissing you solely on grounds of illness. This is known as the opzegverbod tijdens ziekte (prohibition on dismissal during illness). There are limited exceptions: if your company closes entirely, or if you refuse to co-operate with reintegration without valid reason, your dismissal protection may be weakened. But in normal circumstances, your position is secure while you are ill, and any notice of dismissal issued during sick leave is void. This protection applies equally to employees on permanent contracts and those on fixed-term contracts, although for the latter it runs only for the remainder of the contract duration.

After two years: the WIA assessment

When two years of illness have elapsed, the UWV carries out an assessment under the Wet werk en inkomen naar arbeidsvermogen (WIA). If you are found to be more than 35 per cent incapacitated for work, you may be entitled to a government benefit: the IVA for full and permanent incapacity, or the WGA for partial or temporary incapacity. If your incapacity is below 35 per cent, you receive no WIA benefit and are expected to find work independently. At this point your employer may also give notice of termination, subject to the standard dismissal rules. For expats on a sponsored work visa, it is worth consulting an employment lawyer or your employer's HR team well before the two-year mark, as long-term incapacity can have implications for your residence permit status.

Disagreeing with the company doctor

The bedrijfsarts assesses what you are functionally able to do, and their opinion drives the reintegration process. Employees often assume this assessment is final. It is not.

If you believe the company doctor has misjudged your capacity — in either direction — you can request a second opinion from another company doctor, and you can apply to the UWV for an independent expert judgement (deskundigenoordeel). That UWV opinion carries real weight in any subsequent dispute, and it is available to both employee and employer.

Use it rather than simply refusing to cooperate. Declining to engage with reintegration can justify suspending your sick pay, whereas formally contesting the assessment protects your position while the disagreement is resolved.

Falling ill while abroad

Expats frequently become ill while visiting family abroad, and the rules still apply. You must report sick on the first day exactly as you would at home, and you must remain reachable and available for assessment.

Employers can require you to return, or to be assessed locally, and prolonged unreachability can put your sick pay at risk. If you fall ill abroad, tell your employer immediately, give them a working phone number and address, and ask explicitly what they require rather than assuming distance excuses the usual obligations.

If you are on a temporary contract or agency work

Protection is strong but its duration is not unlimited, and this is where expats on fixed-term arrangements get caught. Dismissal protection during illness runs only to the end of the contract — when a fixed-term contract expires while you are ill, it simply ends.

At that point responsibility generally transfers to the UWV rather than the employer, and you claim sickness benefit through them. The practical consequence is a change of counterparty, of payment level, and of process, at the least convenient possible moment. If your contract end date is approaching while you are on sick leave, find out in advance what happens rather than discovering it when payments stop.

What illness means for your residence permit

This is the expat-specific dimension the Dutch system is not designed around. Many residence permits — the highly skilled migrant permit in particular — are tied to continued employment above a salary threshold.

Sick pay at 70% can drop you below the threshold your permit requires, and if long-term illness ends the employment relationship the permit basis disappears with it. This does not usually bite immediately, and there are search periods and alternative routes, but it needs handling deliberately.

If illness looks likely to extend beyond a few months, take immigration advice early — well before the two-year mark, not after. The interaction between long-term sickness, the WIA assessment and permit renewal is genuinely complex, and options are far wider while you are still employed.

faq.q: Does my employer have the right to ask what illness I have?
faq.a: No. Your employer may ask how long you expect to be absent and how to reach you, but they are not permitted to ask for or record your diagnosis. Under Dutch privacy law and the GDPR, medical details go only to the company doctor (bedrijfsarts), who reports back to your employer purely in terms of what you are functionally able to do — not why.

faq.q: How much of my salary do I get while on sick leave?
faq.a: Dutch law guarantees at least 70% of your last-earned wage for up to two years, and during the first year that 70% must be at least the statutory minimum wage. Many collective labour agreements (CAO) are more generous, commonly paying 100% in year one and 70% in year two. There is no unpaid waiting period at the start of a sick period.

faq.q: Can I be fired while I am off sick?
faq.a: Generally no. The opzegverbod tijdens ziekte prohibits dismissal on the grounds of illness for up to two years, and notice issued during sick leave is void. Narrow exceptions exist — for example if the company closes entirely, or if you refuse to co-operate with reintegration without good reason. On a fixed-term contract the protection runs only to the end of the contract.

faq.q: What if I disagree with the company doctor?
faq.a: Their assessment isn't final. You can request a second opinion from another company doctor, and you can ask the UWV for an independent expert judgement, which carries real weight in a dispute. Contest it formally rather than refusing to cooperate — declining to engage with reintegration can justify suspending your sick pay.

faq.q: What happens if I'm ill when my temporary contract ends?
faq.a: The contract simply ends — dismissal protection during illness only runs to the end of a fixed term. Responsibility generally transfers to the UWV, and you claim sickness benefit through them instead of your employer. Find out what that means for you in advance rather than when payments change.

faq.q: Can long-term illness affect my residence permit?
faq.a: Yes, and it's the dimension the system isn't designed around. Permits like the highly skilled migrant one are tied to employment above a salary threshold, and sick pay at 70% can fall below it — while long-term illness ending the employment removes the permit's basis entirely. Take immigration advice early, well before the two-year WIA point.

title: Dutch citizenship in 2026: naturalisation rules and a looming change
excerpt: Five years of residence still applies today, but a bill would raise it to ten and the language bar from A2 to B1. Here's what's required now, how naturalisation differs from the option procedure, what renunciation really involves, and how to keep your residence clock intact.
body:
Becoming a Dutch citizen has, for decades, followed a fairly stable rule: five years of uninterrupted legal residence, alongside proof of integration, was usually enough to apply. That baseline is now under review. In late 2025 the Dutch cabinet published a draft bill that would extend the standard naturalisation period from five years to ten, and by mid-2026 the proposal was working its way through parliament rather than sitting on a shelf. For expats weighing whether and when to apply for Dutch citizenship, understanding both the current rules and the direction of travel matters.

What naturalisation requires today

Under the rules still in force in 2026, most applicants can apply for naturalisation after five consecutive years of legal residence in the Netherlands. You also need to satisfy the civic integration requirement — either the inburgering exam or an approved diploma exemption — and demonstrate Dutch language ability, currently assessed at A2 level for most applicants. Spouses and registered partners of Dutch nationals benefit from a shorter route: three years of residence and cohabitation is generally sufficient, and in some cases naturalisation can even be arranged from abroad. Dual nationality is not automatically permitted; most applicants must renounce their existing nationality, subject to a list of exemptions that includes people who cannot renounce under the law of their country of origin.

The proposed extension to ten years

The bill put forward by the Ministry of Justice and Security would raise the standard residence requirement from five years to ten. The stated aim, according to State Secretary Arno Rutte, is to ensure applicants have built deeper and more durable ties to the Netherlands before acquiring citizenship. The spousal route would also change: the three-year period for partners of Dutch nationals would rise to five years, and naturalisation from abroad for spouses and former Dutch nationals would be abolished entirely. The language bar is also expected to rise, from A2 to B1, regardless of how the residence-period debate concludes.

Other changes buried in the draft

Beyond the headline five-to-ten change, the bill closes a route some applicants have used to hold dual nationality: renouncing Dutch citizenship shortly after naturalising, then reclaiming it a year later through the option procedure for former Dutch nationals, which does not carry the same renunciation requirement. Under the new bill, anyone who reclaims citizenship this way would face the renunciation requirement again, even retroactively for applications not yet decided. The bill would also remove an existing exception that lets some long-term residents naturalise after just two uninterrupted years, provided they have accumulated ten years of lawful residence in total. If adopted as drafted, that shortcut disappears.

Where the proposal stands

The bill went through public internet consultation until 1 December 2025 and has since been reviewed by the Council of State before formal submission to the Tweede Kamer (House of Representatives). Parliamentary planning documents pointed to a plenary debate in the first quarter of 2026, though timelines for legislation of this kind routinely slip. Crucially, the proposal originated under a caretaker cabinet before the general election of 29 October 2025, so its ultimate fate depends on the priorities of the coalition that followed. As of mid-2026, the current five-year rule remains the law — nothing has changed yet for anyone applying today.

The bill is not expected to apply retroactively for the core five-to-ten change. Applications submitted, and naturalisation procedures already under way, before any new law takes effect would continue to be assessed under the existing five-year rule. That detail is the single most consequential piece of information for anyone currently eligible or close to eligible.

What this means if you are working toward citizenship

If you have already passed the five-year mark, or expect to within the next year or two, it is worth treating your application as time-sensitive rather than assuming you can apply whenever suits you. Immigration solicitors have warned that a rush of applications is likely as the bill progresses, which could extend waiting times for integration exams and naturalisation appointments in the larger cities, particularly Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and The Hague. If you are relying on the shorter spousal route, or on the ten-year residence exception that the bill would abolish, the case for applying sooner rather than later is stronger still. Anyone with a gap in their residence permit history — a so-called residence gap — should also treat the proposal as a reason to resolve it now, since an uninterrupted record becomes more valuable the longer the required period gets. Applying for a permanent residence permit at the five-year mark is worth considering even if you are not yet ready to naturalise, since it prevents a residence gap forming while you wait.

Getting advice

Because the rules are in flux and the consequences of missing a deadline are real, this is an area where a short consultation with an immigration solicitor is worth the cost for anyone close to the threshold. Dutch immigration law firms have been tracking the bill closely and can advise on residence gaps, the option procedure, and whether it makes sense to apply now under the current rules rather than wait. For expats who are years away from meeting even the current five-year threshold, the practical takeaway is simpler: keep your residence permit continuous, keep records of your address history, and revisit the question once the bill's progress through parliament becomes clearer.

Naturalisation or option: two different routes

Dutch citizenship is acquired through one of two procedures, and applicants regularly pursue the wrong one.

Naturalisation is the general route: the residence period, the integration exam, the language requirement, and in most cases renunciation of your existing nationality. It is discretionary, takes up to a year to decide, and carries a substantial fee.

The option procedure is a faster, cheaper declaration available to defined groups — people born in the Netherlands who have lived there since birth, certain long-term residents who arrived as minors, former Dutch nationals, and some partners in specific circumstances. Where you qualify it is markedly simpler and decided in a matter of months rather than a year.

Because the criteria are narrow and technical, it is worth checking whether you fall inside the option procedure before assuming naturalisation is your only path — particularly if you arrived as a child or previously held Dutch nationality.

What renunciation actually means in practice

The requirement to give up your existing nationality is the part applicants most underestimate, because it is not a formality on a Dutch form — it is a separate legal process with your own country, conducted on their timetable and at their cost.

Exemptions exist and are broader than commonly assumed. They generally cover people whose country does not permit renunciation at all, refugees, spouses of Dutch nationals, those born in the Netherlands, and cases where renunciation would cause disproportionate harm — losing inheritance rights or property ownership in the country of origin, for instance. Whether your situation falls inside an exemption is genuinely case-specific.

Think through the consequences before starting. Losing your original nationality can affect the right to live and work there, property and inheritance rights, visa-free travel on that passport, and your children's citizenship. These are not reversible on a change of mind.

Cost, timing and the ceremony

Naturalisation carries a substantial application fee — several hundred euros for a single applicant, more for couples, with reduced rates for children applying alongside a parent. It is payable up front and is not refunded if your application is refused, which is a strong argument for confirming eligibility before filing.

Applications are submitted at your gemeente, which forwards them to the IND. The statutory decision period runs up to a year and can be extended. Once approved, citizenship is not acquired until you attend a naturalisation ceremony and make the declaration of solidarity — municipalities hold these periodically, and missing yours delays acquisition until the next one.

Keeping the residence clock intact

The residence requirement demands uninterrupted legal residence, and that is a technical condition rather than a loose one. Extended absences can break it, gaps between residence permits can break it, and a lapse in municipal registration can call the whole period into question.

Two habits protect you. Keep continuous registration and continuous valid residence status, renewing permits well before expiry rather than at the edge. And keep your own records — permit copies, registration history, evidence of presence — because you may be asked to demonstrate a period the authorities cannot fully reconstruct themselves.

If a long posting abroad is likely, take advice before you go. Some absences are tolerated and others reset the clock, and the difference is worth knowing in advance rather than discovering at application.

faq.q: How many years of residence do I need for Dutch citizenship right now?
faq.a: Five years of continuous legal residence remains the standard requirement today. A bill has been proposed to extend this to ten years, but a proposal is not law — until it is actually passed and in force, applications continue to be assessed under the current five-year rule.

faq.q: Should I apply now or wait to see what happens with the ten-year proposal?
faq.a: If you already meet today's requirements, there is a clear argument for not delaying, since applications are assessed under the rules in force when you apply. If you are still some years from eligibility, the timing question is genuinely uncertain and worth raising with an immigration lawyer rather than guessing — this guide cannot tell you how the bill will land.

faq.q: Do I have to give up my current nationality?
faq.a: The Netherlands restricts dual nationality, and renunciation of your existing citizenship is required in many cases, though exemptions exist for certain circumstances. Because the exemptions are specific and the consequences permanent, confirm how the rules apply to your own nationality with the IND before starting an application.

faq.q: What's the difference between naturalisation and the option procedure?
faq.a: Naturalisation is the general route — residence period, integration exam, language requirement, usually renunciation — and takes up to a year. The option procedure is a faster, cheaper declaration open to defined groups, including people born in the Netherlands, some who arrived as minors, and former Dutch nationals. Check whether you qualify for option before assuming naturalisation is your only path.

faq.q: What does giving up my original nationality actually involve?
faq.a: A separate legal process with your own country, on their timetable and at their cost — not a Dutch formality. Exemptions are broader than people assume, covering countries that don't permit renunciation, refugees, spouses of Dutch nationals, and cases of disproportionate harm such as losing inheritance or property rights. Consider the knock-on effects on residence, property and your children's status first; they aren't reversible.

faq.q: Can a period abroad break my residence clock?
faq.a: Yes. The requirement is uninterrupted legal residence, and extended absences, gaps between permits, or a lapse in municipal registration can all jeopardise it. Renew permits well before expiry, keep registration continuous, and keep your own records. If a long posting abroad is coming, take advice before you go rather than at application.

title: AOV disability insurance for the self-employed in the Netherlands
excerpt: Self-employed workers in the Netherlands have no state sick pay and no disability cover. Here's what AOV actually costs, the own-occupation clause that decides whether your claim pays, how the tax relief works, and why applying while healthy matters more than the premium.
body:
Self-employment in the Netherlands is straightforward to set up, but it comes with one gap that catches many expat freelancers off guard: there is no automatic income protection if you fall ill or become unable to work. Employees are covered by law. The self-employed, or zzp'ers, are not, unless they arrange it themselves. Understanding the AOV (arbeidsongeschiktheidsverzekering, or occupational disability insurance) is one of the more important pieces of financial planning for anyone running their own business here.

No employer, no automatic safety net

If you work under a Dutch employment contract and fall sick, your employer is obliged to continue paying at least 70% of your salary for up to two years (loondoorbetaling bij ziekte). After that, the WIA (Wet werk en inkomen naar arbeidsvermogen) can provide a longer-term disability benefit. None of this applies if you are registered as self-employed with the Kamer van Koophandel. There is no employer to fall back on, and the state disability scheme does not extend to zzp'ers. In practice, this means an illness or injury that stops you working can end your income overnight, with only the Bijstand (social assistance) safety net as a last resort, and that comes with strict asset and partner-income tests that exclude many people.

What an AOV policy actually covers

A private AOV is an insurance contract you take out with a Dutch insurer, typically covering a percentage of your declared income if you become unable to work due to illness or disability. You choose an eigen risicotermijn, or waiting period, before payments begin, usually somewhere between one month and a year, with a longer waiting period lowering your premium. You also choose the insured benefit amount, the percentage of your income the policy pays out, and the end age of the cover. Insurers will ask detailed health questions before accepting you, and pre-existing conditions can lead to exclusions, a loading on the premium, or in some cases a refusal to insure you at all, which is worth bearing in mind if you plan to switch policies later.

What it costs, and why premiums vary so much

There is no single price for an AOV. Premiums are calculated individually based on your age, occupation, health history, the waiting period you select, and how much income you want insured. A physically demanding trade will generally cost more to insure than desk-based freelance work. As a rough benchmark, the government's own proposed mandatory scheme, discussed below, priced its basic premium at around 6.5% of income, capped at approximately €195 a month in 2026 — useful context, though private market premiums for a comparable level of cover can sit above or below that figure depending on your profile. The only reliable way to know your own cost is to request quotes from two or three insurers or an independent adviser (assurantietussenpersoon).

Broodfonds and other alternatives

Not every self-employed person in the Netherlands buys formal insurance. A well-established alternative is the broodfonds, a mutual support arrangement in which a group of self-employed people, often numbering several dozen, each pay into a personal savings pot and agree to gift money to any member who falls ill, up to an agreed monthly amount for a set number of years. It is not insurance in the legal sense — there is no underwriting and no guaranteed payout — but it is popular among freelancers who find formal AOV premiums prohibitive, particularly those in creative or lower-income professions. Others simply build a large cash buffer instead, though this only offers meaningful protection against short absences rather than a long-term disability.

The mandatory AOV that keeps being postponed

For several years, the Dutch government has been developing legislation, the Wet basisverzekering arbeidsongeschiktheid zelfstandigen (Wet Baz), to make a basic disability insurance compulsory for anyone registered as self-employed for income tax purposes. Under the current proposal, the mandatory scheme would pay out up to 70% of a claimant's income, capped at 100% of the statutory minimum wage. The obligation was originally pencilled in for 2027 but has since been pushed back, with 2030 now the earliest expected start date, and the exact timing remains unconfirmed. If you take out a private AOV before the relevant reference date once it is set, you may qualify for more flexible transitional terms under the eventual law, so it is worth keeping an eye on developments even if you already have private cover.

Deciding what is right for you

There is no universally correct answer here. A freelancer with dependants, a mortgage, and no savings buffer has a very different risk profile from someone early in their career with modest fixed costs. Get quotes from a few insurers, ask an independent adviser to compare options rather than relying on a single insurer's recommendation, and weigh the premium against what a year or more without income would actually mean for your household. Whatever you decide, deciding deliberately, rather than defaulting to no cover because the paperwork is unfamiliar, is the important part.

The variables that actually set your premium

Quotes vary enormously between people, and the reason is that you are choosing the shape of the policy as much as buying a fixed product. Four levers do most of the work.

The waiting period (eigen risicotermijn) is how long you must be unable to work before payments start — commonly anywhere from two weeks to a year. Extending it cuts the premium sharply, and is the main lever for anyone with savings to bridge the gap.

The end age matters because cover to state pension age costs considerably more than cover to 60. The insured amount is usually capped at a share of recent income rather than anything you choose. And the occupational definition — discussed below — is the one most people ignore and the one most likely to matter at claim time.

Own occupation or any occupation: the clause that decides your claim

This is the most important term in the contract. A policy written on own occupation (beroepsarbeidsongeschiktheid) pays when you cannot do your own job. A policy written more loosely can decline if you are capable of some other work.

For a specialised freelancer the difference is everything. A surgeon with a hand injury, or a photographer who loses fine vision, may be entirely unable to practise while remaining capable of office work. Under a narrow definition, that is not a claim. Cheaper policies frequently achieve their price precisely here.

Read this clause before comparing premiums, because two quotes with the same monthly cost can be selling fundamentally different products.

Tax treatment

AOV premiums are generally deductible against income tax, which reduces the real cost meaningfully — a policy costing €250 a month is materially cheaper after relief. The corollary is that benefits paid out are generally taxable as income.

This is the right way round for most people, and it means comparing a premium against gross income overstates the burden. Our tax filing guide covers where this sits on the return.

Applying: medical underwriting and why timing matters

AOV is medically underwritten. Expect a health questionnaire and, depending on age and cover, a medical examination. Insurers can decline, load the premium, or — most commonly — exclude specific conditions.

The practical consequence: apply while you are healthy. An existing back problem, a treated mental health condition, or a recent injury will typically be excluded permanently, and those exclusions frequently cover the exact risks most likely to stop you working. Freelancers who postpone cover until they can afford it often find the version they can then buy excludes what they most needed.

Answer the questionnaire completely and honestly. Non-disclosure is the standard reason claims fail years later, and an insurer reviewing a claim will look at your medical history in detail.

faq.q: Is AOV insurance mandatory for freelancers in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Not currently. A mandatory scheme for self-employed workers has been proposed and repeatedly postponed, so as things stand cover is entirely voluntary. If you are self-employed and have no policy, you have no automatic income protection if you become unable to work.

faq.q: What does an AOV policy typically cost?
faq.a: There is no single price — premiums are individually calculated from your age, occupation, health history, chosen waiting period, and how much income you insure. Physically demanding trades cost more to insure than desk-based work. For rough context, the proposed mandatory scheme priced its basic premium at around 6.5% of income, capped at roughly €195 a month in 2026, though private quotes can sit above or below that. Request quotes from two or three insurers or an independent adviser.

faq.q: What is a broodfonds and is it a substitute for AOV?
faq.a: A broodfonds is a small mutual group whose members make monthly contributions and support each other with gifted payments during illness. It is a genuine alternative for shorter absences and is considerably cheaper, but it is not insurance and typically covers a limited period — usually up to two years — so it does not replace an AOV for long-term or permanent incapacity.

faq.q: What's the difference between own-occupation and any-occupation cover?
faq.a: The most important term in the contract. Own-occupation pays when you cannot do your own job; a looser definition can decline if you're capable of some other work. A photographer losing fine vision may be unable to practise while still able to do office work — under a narrow definition that isn't a claim. Cheaper policies often get their price exactly here.

faq.q: Are AOV premiums tax deductible?
faq.a: Generally yes, against income tax, which cuts the real cost meaningfully — so comparing the headline premium against gross income overstates the burden. The flip side is that benefits paid out are generally taxable as income.

faq.q: Should I wait until I can afford better cover?
faq.a: Usually not. AOV is medically underwritten, and insurers commonly exclude existing conditions permanently. Freelancers who postpone often find the policy they can eventually buy excludes precisely the risks most likely to stop them working. Applying while healthy is worth more than a slightly better product later.

title: Moving to the Netherlands: the arrival checklist, in order
excerpt: Registration, BSN, DigiD, banking and health insurance have to happen in a specific order, and three of them carry legal deadlines. Here is the sequence that actually works, with the deadlines that matter.
body:
Almost everything that makes the first months in the Netherlands stressful comes down to sequencing. A handful of essential steps have to happen in a particular order, several have legal deadlines attached, and each one tends to be a prerequisite for the next. Miss the order and you end up stuck — unable to open a bank account because you have no BSN, unable to get a BSN because you have not registered, unable to register because you have no address.

This is the sequence, with the deadlines that actually carry consequences. Each step links to the full guide for that topic.

Before you arrive: secure an address

Everything downstream depends on having a registerable Dutch address, so this is the real first step even though it happens before you land. A great many gemeenten will not register you at a short-term holiday let, and some landlords explicitly forbid registration in the tenancy agreement — a clause worth checking before you sign anything. If you are arriving without permanent housing, look for a rental that explicitly permits registration (inschrijving toegestaan), even if it is temporary.

See: renting an apartment as an expat and choosing which city to live in.

Step 1 — Register at your gemeente (within 5 days)

If you are staying longer than four months, Dutch law requires you to register at your local municipality within five days of arriving. In practice gemeenten cannot always offer an appointment inside that window, so the sensible approach is to book the appointment the moment you know your arrival date and keep evidence that you tried to comply. Bring your passport, your tenancy agreement, and a legalised birth certificate — the birth certificate requirement catches people out constantly, because obtaining an apostilled copy from your home country can take weeks.

See: registering at the gemeente, step by step.

Step 2 — Receive your BSN

Your citizen service number is issued as part of that registration appointment. Some gemeenten hand it over on the spot as a paper certificate; others post it to your address within five to ten business days. Nothing much can proceed without it: it is required for employment, tax, healthcare, and most banking.

See: the BSN explained.

Step 3 — Apply for DigiD

DigiD is the national digital identity used to log in to tax, healthcare, benefits, and municipal services. You can only apply once you have a BSN, and activation runs through a letter posted to your registered address, typically arriving within about five business days. Apply as soon as your BSN comes through, because the wait is unavoidable and a great deal of admin is gated behind it.

See: getting DigiD as an expat.

Step 4 — Open a bank account

Most traditional Dutch banks want a BSN before they will open a current account, which is why this sits after registration rather than before. If you need an account sooner — to receive a first salary, or to pay a deposit — several neobanks with Dutch IBANs will open an account without a BSN, which is a reasonable stopgap while the rest of the paperwork catches up.

See: best bank accounts for expats and opening an account without a BSN.

Step 5 — Take out health insurance (within 4 months)

This is the deadline with the sharpest teeth. Everyone living or working in the Netherlands must hold Dutch basic health insurance within four months of arrival or the start of employment. Miss it and you are enrolled retroactively and charged a penalty premium, so the cost of forgetting is real money rather than an administrative scolding. Cover is backdated to your registration date once you take out a policy, which means the premium you owe starts accruing from arrival regardless of when you get around to it.

See: the complete health insurance guide.

Then, when the essentials are done

With registration, BSN, DigiD, banking, and insurance in place, the remaining setup is comparatively relaxed and has no hard deadlines. Sort out internet and energy, pick up a mobile plan, and — if you drive — start the process of exchanging your licence, which has its own timing rules worth reading early.

If you are arriving for skilled work, check whether you qualify for the 30% ruling before your first payroll run — the application is made through your employer and is significantly easier to handle at the start of employment than retrospectively.

A realistic timeline

For most people the essentials take somewhere between three and eight weeks end to end, and the pacing is set almost entirely by appointment availability at the gemeente and by postal delivery of the DigiD activation letter. Neither can be rushed. What you can control is starting early: book the gemeente appointment before you fly, and order a legalised birth certificate well in advance. Those two decisions remove most of the delay that expats complain about.

infographic.alt: Checklist for your first weeks in the Netherlands: register at the gemeente within 5 days, get your BSN, activate DigiD, open a bank account, and take out health insurance within 4 months.
infographic.caption: The five steps with real deadlines, in the order they have to happen.

faq.q: What is the very first thing I should do when I arrive?
faq.a: Register at your gemeente. Dutch law gives you five days from arrival if you are staying longer than four months, and almost everything else — your BSN, DigiD, a bank account, health insurance — depends on that registration having happened. Book the appointment before you fly if you can.

faq.q: Can I open a Dutch bank account before I have a BSN?
faq.a: Not usually with a traditional Dutch bank, which is why this step sits after registration. Several neobanks offering Dutch IBANs will open an account without a BSN, which works as a stopgap for receiving a first salary or paying a deposit while your registration completes.

faq.q: What happens if I miss the four-month health insurance deadline?
faq.a: You are enrolled retroactively and charged a penalty premium on top of the backdated contributions. Cover is backdated to your registration date regardless of when you take out the policy, so delaying does not save you the premium — it just adds a fine to it.
